strengths: Clear and well-motivated formulation: image-based motion forecasting as conditional generation of quasi-dense trajectory grids, which naturally handles stochastic/multi-modal futures unlike prior regression-based point-track forecasters (ATM, Tra-MoE).

Comprehensive evaluation across regression baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE), a generative trajectory baseline (Track2Act, trained under a carefully matched protocol), generative image-to-video models (WAN, SVD, LTX, DynamicCrafter, including fine-tuned variants), and a real-world dataset (Physics101), plus a user study.

The controlled modality ablation (Table 6: identical architecture/training, only RGB vs. trajectory outputs) is a well-designed experiment that directly supports the central claim that pixel generation overhead, not model capacity/dimensionality, causes implausible motion in video generators.
Thoughtful metrics: FVMD and image-wise FVMD, best-of-K MSE, and a novel rigidity-inspired LRTL score, with a sanity-check experiment (Table 21) verifying metric sensitivity.

Thorough ablations (VAE vs. raw coordinates with mode-collapse analysis, model scale, CoTracker supervision vs. GT trajectories), extensive reproducibility details (hyperparameters, compute budgets, evaluation cost), plus ethics and LLM-use statements.
Practically attractive efficiency profile: ~1-2s inference and <1M-220M parameters vs. multi-billion-parameter video generators taking minutes per sample.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method largely repackages known components (Latte/DiT-style transformer, beta-VAE, rectified flow) applied to trajectories rather than pixels; the architectural contribution is incremental.

Evaluation is dominated by synthetic data (Kubric, LIBERO, Physion); the real-world validation (Physics101 with a single CoTracker pseudo-ground-truth sample per condition) is limited and uses a potentially noisy evaluation target, weakening the claim of superiority over WAN on real data.

Short prediction horizon (24 frames) and 256x256 resolution limit applicability to longer-horizon, higher-resolution motion forecasting; the authors acknowledge reduced conditioning resolution degrades accuracy near object boundaries.

Several key metrics (LRTL, image-wise FVMD variants, best-of-K with simulated multi-future setups) are introduced by the authors; while sanity-checked, they are not externally validated and could favor the proposed method's inductive biases.

The comparison to video generators, while extensive, may partly reflect a domain mismatch: these models were pre-trained on natural video, and even fine-tuned on small synthetic datasets they may not be expected to excel—making the 'video generators fail at physics' headline claim somewhat unsurprising and narrower than suggested.
Some framing risks over-claiming: conclusions about world models and video generators rest on simple simulated scenarios (falling blocks) and a small real-world set.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and timely question: whether video generators are effective world models for motion forecasting, or whether direct trajectory generation is preferable.

The formulation of motion forecasting as conditional generative modeling of quasi-dense point trajectory grids is clean, and the architectural parallel to modern video generators (latent flow matching on a trajectory VAE built from Latte/DiT blocks) makes the comparison to video generators unusually well-controlled.

The evaluation is fairly broad: regression baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE), a diffusion trajectory baseline (Track2Act), several large-scale video generators (WAN, SVD, LTX-Video, DynamicCraft), a training-free baseline (MotionModes), plus a user study.

The key modality ablation (Section 4.3) is the most convincing part: training identical RGB and trajectory generators with matched latent shapes, showing RGB VAEs reconstruct nearly perfectly (Table 7), which credibly isolates the output modality rather than architecture or capacity as the source of motion errors.

Useful supplementary material: CoTracker-based trajectory evaluation (Table 20), a sanity check that ground truth predicts itself better than CoTracker predictions (Table 21), model scale and VAE ablations, mode-collapse analysis (Fig. 7), hyperparameter tables, and compute estimates — all good for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a standard latent flow matching pipeline (beta-VAE + rectified flow with Latte-style DiT blocks) applied to point trajectories. The main novelty is the problem reformulation and the empirical finding, not a new modeling technique.

The empirical scope is narrow. Quantitative results are dominated by synthetic Kubric scenes with geometric primitives; real-world evaluation (Physics101) uses a single CoTracker-extracted pseudo-ground-truth sample per condition and compares against only one fine-tuned baseline (WAN), and the Physion real-world results are purely qualitative.

Comparisons on LIBERO against ATM and Tra-MoE rely on CoTracker pseudo-labels as ground truth and an MSE protocol with fairness caveats (different point sets, filtering schemes, and conditioning), making the reported gains harder to interpret as motion-forecasting superiority.

Prediction horizons are short (16-30 frames) and scenarios are simple (falling blocks, ramps, springs); the claim that this exposes limitations of 'world models' trained on billions of videos could be over-interpreted given the domain gap and limited temporal extent.

The custom metrics (FVMD, FVMD (S), Best-of-K, LRTL) are adapted or proposed by the authors, and their validation (Table 21) is limited; LRTL's rank-5 truncation threshold appears arbitrary and its sensitivity is not analyzed.
The user study is small (20 users, 16 scenes) and only covers two fine-tuned video baselines; no statistical significance testing is reported.

Several important design questions are left under-explored: the VAE ablation is inconsistent across datasets (worse with VAE on Physics101), and the trajectory VAE's behavior for long-horizon or camera-motion-heavy scenes (where the grid formulation is most ambiguous) is not analyzed.
Given the strong framing in the introduction about world models and physical priors, the practical utility of quasi-dense trajectory generation (e.g., downstream robotics tasks) is not demonstrated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: image-based motion forecasting as conditional generation of quasi-dense point trajectory grids, which naturally handles the inherent multi-modality of the task (unlike deterministic regressors such as ATM and Tra-MoE).

Strong and comprehensive empirical comparisons: the method outperforms regression baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE), a generative trajectory baseline (Track2Act), a training-free motion method (MotionModes), and several state-of-the-art video generators (WAN, SVD, LTX-Video, DynamicCrafter), both with and without fine-tuning the video generators on the target domain.

The modality ablation (Table 6) is a genuinely compelling controlled experiment: by fixing architecture, latent dimensionality, and training procedure and only switching RGB vs. trajectories, the authors convincingly isolate that the failure of video generators on motion prediction stems from the overhead of pixel generation rather than model capacity or pre-training. This is a valuable, transferable insight for the world-model community.

Thoughtful evaluation design: the paper uses complementary metrics (FVMD, FVMD(S), Best-of-K, LRTL for rigidity), explicitly verifies metric sensitivity with a GT-vs-GT sanity check (Table 21), and includes a user study for human plausibility assessment.

Good breadth across domains: synthetic physics (Kubric, in- and out-of-distribution), robotics (LIBERO), Physion, and real-world data (Physics101), plus qualitative evidence of synthetic-to-real generalization.

Strong ablations (VAE vs. raw coordinates with mode-collapse analysis in Fig. 7, model scale, CoTracker-estimated vs. GT targets, text conditioning) and excellent reproducibility detail (full hyperparameter tables, hardware, compute estimates, evaluation protocols for all baselines).
Efficient: the model is orders of magnitude smaller and faster than the video generators it outperforms, strengthening the practical significance of the claim.
weaknesses: Limited real-world quantitative evaluation: Physics101 comparisons rely on a single CoTracker3 pseudo-ground-truth per initial condition and a single sample per method, which weakens the strength of conclusions on real data; the VAE ablation is also inconsistent on Physics101 (Table 14).
The training and primary evaluation are largely synthetic; the paper acknowledges limited in-the-wild generalization, so the practical impact at scale remains to be demonstrated.

Some comparisons involve substantially different compute scales (e.g., 14B-parameter WAN vs. a 220M model fine-tuned on the target domain); although fine-tuning partially mitigates this, the framing 'small model beats billion-video world models' should be interpreted with care.

Best-of-K / Min metrics can favor stochastic methods with higher diversity; while MeanT and Mean variants are reported and support the claims, the choice of k and aggregation schemes requires careful reading.

Conceptually, the method is a fairly direct adaptation of latent flow matching (Latte-style DiT + VAE) to the trajectory modality; the novelty lies mainly in the formulation, modality analysis, and empirical findings rather than in new generative modeling techniques.
The user study is small in scale (20 users, 16 scenes), limiting statistical power.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question — whether large-scale video generators act as effective world models for motion forecasting — and provides a well-motivated alternative: conditional generation of quasi-dense point trajectories via latent flow matching, rather than regressing sparse active points or generating pixels.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: multiple datasets (Kubric in/out-of-distribution, LIBERO, Physics101, Cityscapes, Physion), multiple baseline families (deterministic regressors ATM/Tra-MoE, generative Track2Act, MotionModes, and fine-tuned video generators WAN/SVD/DynamicCrafter/LTX), plus a user study with ELO scores.

The controlled modality ablation (Table 6) is the strongest technical contribution: holding the architecture fixed and switching only RGB vs. trajectory latents (and joint RGB+tracks) cleanly supports the central hypothesis that pixel-space generation introduces overhead that harms motion plausibility, with VAE reconstruction checks and CoTracker sanity checks to rule out confounds.

Careful attention to fairness in comparisons: baselines get their own conditioning signals (text), evaluation point selection follows baseline filtering schemes, the authors report MeanT/Mean/Min aggregations, and they train baselines on the same data/hardware/time budget.

Good ablations on design choices (VAE vs. raw coordinates with a mode-collapse analysis, model scale, trajectory grid density, source of trajectory supervision), and detailed reproducibility information including hardware, hyperparameters, and evaluation cost (~500 GPU hours).
The method is dramatically cheaper and faster than video-generator baselines (Table 22), strengthening practical significance for robotics/planning applications.
weaknesses: The core method is architecturally conventional: a Latte-style spatio-temporal transformer VAE + rectified flow, applied to a trajectory representation. The novelty lies mostly in the formulation (dense trajectory grid generation) and the empirical findings, not in the generative modeling technique itself.

The headline claim that video generators struggle with physical motion is already well documented (Physics-IQ, VideoPhy, Kang et al. — which the paper itself cites in Appendix F), so this finding alone is not new; the added value is the modality-overhead explanation, which rests primarily on one controlled experiment on one dataset family (Kubric).

The Kubric evaluation is based on only 16 scenes (1,024 rollouts), raising concerns about statistical strength of the distributional metrics (FVMD, FVMD(S), LRTL), especially given that the authors themselves show these metrics are sensitive to sample count (Table 24). No error bars or significance tests are reported anywhere.

Real-world results rely on CoTracker3 pseudo-ground truth for both training and evaluation, which risks circularity: trajectory-based methods are evaluated against a tracker whose failure modes they do not share, while video generators are penalized twice (generation error + tracking error). The Physics101 and Cityscapes comparisons may thus be systematically biased in favor of the proposed approach.

There are minor internal inconsistencies (e.g., LRTL for Ours(L) reported as 14.1 in Table 3 but 14.6 in Table 14; metric scales in Table 17 are orders of magnitude smaller than in Table 3, presumably a different normalization that is not explained), which undermine confidence in the numbers.
The user study is small (20 users, 16 scenes) and evaluates only coarse preference; the user study compares only against fine-tuned SVD/WAN, not against Track2Act or MotionModes.

Some comparisons are not fully like-for-like: the proposed method uses DINOv2 patch-token cross-attention conditioning while Track2Act uses a small ResNet single-vector conditioning, and the authors attribute Track2Act's loss partly to this conditioning difference rather than the generative-vs-regression or dense-vs-sparse distinction — making the attribution of gains to specific factors less crisp.

Scope of generalization is limited: training is mostly synthetic, and the real-world in-the-wild claim (Physion-to-real) is purely qualitative; the paper's practical impact claim (policy learning, model-based control) is not tested downstream (no control/policy experiments).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: casting single-image motion forecasting as conditional generative modeling of quasi-dense trajectory grids is a sensible and well-argued framing, and the paper articulates the connection to video generators effectively.

The modality ablation (Table 6), where the same architecture is trained with RGB vs. trajectory latents (and a joint variant), is the paper's most convincing experiment and provides genuine evidence for the claim that pixel generation overhead harms motion plausibility.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: comparisons against regression baselines (ATM, Tra-MoE), generative trajectory methods (Track2Act, MotionModes), and multiple fine-tuned video generators across Kubric, LIBERO, Physics101, and Cityscapes, plus a user study.

The paper is transparent about many weaknesses in its own evaluation (single ground truth, pseudo-labels from CoTracker3, coarse distributional metrics) and includes thoughtful ablations (VAE vs. raw coordinates with mode-collapse analysis, grid density, model scale, CoTracker-sourced targets).
Reproducibility is addressed thoroughly: detailed hyperparameters, hardware, training times, and evaluation cost are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is a fairly direct application of established components (beta-VAE latent space + rectified flow matching + Latte/DiT-style transformer with gated cross-attention to DINOv2 features) to a new output modality. No new training technique or architectural insight is contributed; the contribution is primarily empirical re-framing.

Some headline comparisons feel structurally unfair to the video generators: models like WAN 1.3B/14B are fine-tuned on a small, narrow Kubric dataset with compute matched to a much smaller trajectory model, and are then evaluated by extracting tracks with CoTracker3. The conclusion that 'video generators cannot serve as world models for motion' may be an artifact of this setup rather than a fundamental limitation; the paper's claims here are stronger than the evidence.

The evaluation protocol favors the proposed generative approach: Best-of-K/Min metrics reward a method with many diverse samples, and the comparison to deterministic regressors using MeanT/Mean/Min mixes incommensurable statistics. With only one (often pseudo-labeled by CoTracker3) ground-truth future on real datasets, MSE comparisons are noisy and heavily dependent on tracker quality.

The Kubric evaluation set is small (16 scenes, 64 rollouts each), and real-world results are mixed: on Physics101 the method wins in only 3/5 scenarios with a modest overall margin (28.62 vs 30.08), and the Physion real-world results are purely qualitative due to data scale.

Only one ground-truth future per initial condition during training means the stochastic formulation is never validated against a true conditional distribution in the real-world setting; the model's claimed ability to capture multimodality is only demonstrated on synthetic data.

Several writing/clarity issues: dense related-work paragraphs with asserted 'limitations' of prior work that the paper does not empirically substantiate, inconsistent metric presentation across tables, and occasional overclaiming (e.g., 'our method substantially outperforms' on results where margins are small).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: image-based motion forecasting cast as conditional generation of quasi-dense point trajectory grids using flow matching, which naturally models uncertainty over multiple possible futures.

Well-designed and convincing modality ablation (Table 6): holding the architecture fixed and switching only the output modality (RGB latents vs. trajectory latents of comparable dimensionality) provides strong experimental evidence for the central claim that RGB generation overhead causes motion implausibility, rather than model capacity or latent size.

Extensive and mostly fair evaluation across five settings (Kubric in/out-of-distribution, LIBERO, Physion, Physics101, Cityscapes), with carefully designed baselines protocols: adapting ATM/Tra-MoE with text conditioning, extending Track2Act's horizon and point count, fine-tuning video generators on-domain, and validating CoTracker3's reliability on their benchmark (Table 23).

Thoughtful metrics beyond regression: Best-of-K MSE, FVMD and a scene-level conditional variant FVMD(S), and a physically grounded rigidity metric (LRTL), plus verification that the metrics are sensitive (Table 24) and complementary.

Useful ablations: effect of VAE vs. raw coordinates (with mode-collapse analysis via sample variance), model scale, grid density, and trajectory source (ground truth vs. CoTracker pseudo-labels), all supporting design choices.
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, training hardware and time, evaluation cost, model sizes, inference cost comparisons, user study materials, and honest limitations section.

Practical significance: trajectory model is orders of magnitude cheaper at inference (2.9s / 1.9GB vs. WAN's 248s / 32GB) while outperforming large fine-tuned video generators, relevant for robotics and world-model applications.
weaknesses: Moderate architectural novelty: the method is a fairly standard combination of VAE latent space + rectified flow + DiT/Latte-style blocks with gated cross-attention; the main novelty lies in the problem formulation and experimental findings rather than in new modeling techniques.

The claim that pretrained video generators are poor world models is partially anticipated by prior work cited in the paper itself (Motamed et al. 2025, Kang et al. 2024, VideoPhy), so the headline finding is confirmatory rather than entirely new; fine-tuning of video baselines on small synthetic datasets may also understate their potential given resource constraints.

Several real-world evaluations rely on pseudo ground truth from CoTracker3 (Physics101, Cityscapes), so results partly measure consistency with one tracker's estimates rather than true motion; only one ground-truth future per initial condition limits distributional evaluation in these settings.
The VAE ablation is inconsistent across datasets (worse with VAE on Physics101, inconclusive on real data), and the justification for emphasizing Kubric/LIBERO results is somewhat post-hoc.
The user study is small in scale (16 scenes, 20 users) and only covers Kubric with fine-tuned SVD/WAN; ELO differences are not accompanied by statistical significance analysis.

Some quantitative gaps are large partly because Best-of-K and Min aggregation inherently favor generative multi-sample methods over deterministic regressors; while MeanT/Mean aggregations mitigate this, the framing could be more balanced.

Main paper results are mostly on synthetic or narrow-domain data (Kubric primitives, LIBERO tabletop); real-world generalization (Physion-to-real) remains qualitative only, as acknowledged in the limitations.
